Coagulation Disorders

Updated Oct 8, 2026 Revision 1.0 7 learning objectives

Learning objectives

  1. LO 1Walk through normal hemostasis, the two faces of thrombin, and how the endothelium both blocks and builds clots.
  2. LO 2Name the cascade factors and use the extrinsic and intrinsic pathways (PT and aPTT) in practice.
  3. LO 3Explain how plasmin breaks down a clot.
  4. LO 4Use the cascade and the coagulation lab tests to work up a bleeding patient.
  5. LO 5Describe hemophilia A and B: cause, who gets it, how it presents, complications and outlook.
  6. LO 6Tell von Willebrand disease apart from hemophilia A by its clinical picture and labs.
  7. LO 7Explain how the Factor V Leiden mutation causes clots and what it does clinically.

MAPBig-picture map of coagulation disorders

LO 1Normal hemostasis, thrombin and the endothelium

Q1. What does secondary hemostasis add to the platelet plug?
  • The platelet plug (primary hemostasis) is weak; it needs protection from the shear stress of flowing blood
  • Secondary hemostasis builds a fibrin mesh that stabilizes the platelet aggregates
  • Platelets are not bystanders: they are vital for thrombin generation and keep thrombin localized to the injury
  • Coagulation "cross-talks" with the immune system and the vascular endothelium
PhaseWhat happens
1Extrinsic and intrinsic pathways make prothrombinase (prothrombin activator, Xa)
2Prothrombinase converts prothrombin → thrombin
3Thrombin converts soluble fibrinogen → insoluble fibrin, the "scaffolding" of the thrombus
Analogy — sandbags and cement

The platelet plug is a wall of sandbags thrown into the breach. Fibrin is the cement poured over them so the current can't wash them away.

Q2. Why is thrombin both a clotting and an anticlotting protein?

Prothrombotic (at the injury)

  • Cleaves fibrinogen → fibrin
  • Activates XIII → cross-links fibrin
  • Feeds back: activates V, VIII, XI
  • Releases FVIII from vWF
  • Activates platelets

Antithrombotic (on intact endothelium)

  • Binds thrombomodulin → loses its clotting function
  • Thrombin–thrombomodulin activates protein C
  • APC + cofactor protein S destroy Va and VIIIa
  • Keeps the clot from spreading onto healthy wall
In-house exam

"Thrombin bound to thrombomodulin" = activates protein C (anticoagulant). Expect thrombin's dual role to be tested.

Step 1

Direct thrombin inhibitors: argatroban, bivalirudin, dabigatran. Heparin works indirectly, through antithrombin.

Q3. How does the endothelium block clots, and how does it promote them?
TargetHealthy endothelium (anti-clot)Injured endothelium (pro-clot)
PlateletsPGI₂, NO, ADPaseReleases vWF, exposes collagen
CoagulationHeparan sulfate (→ antithrombin), thrombomodulin (→ protein C), TFPITissue factor
FibrinolysistPAPAI-1
ToneVasodilationEndothelin
Memory tool

Healthy endothelium is Teflon; injured endothelium is Velcro. Inflamed endothelium (calcified plaque, autoimmune attack) can turn Velcro even without a cut.

Q4. What are the body's natural anticoagulants?
BrakeActionClue when missing
Antithrombin (III)Inhibits Xa and thrombin (also IXa, XIa, XIIa)Heparin doesn't raise the aPTT; nephrotic syndrome
HeparinFrom basophils (and mast cells); potentiates antithrombin—
Antithromboplastin (TFPI)Inhibits tissue factor—
Proteins C + SActivated by thrombin; degrade Va and VIIIaVenous clots; warfarin skin necrosis
High yield

Lose a procoagulant (VIII, IX, XI) → bleeding. Lose or break an anticoagulant (protein C, protein S, FV Leiden) → thrombosis.

Memory tool

Protein C Cancels, protein S Stops: together they shut off V and VIII.

ApplyLO 1 application questions

A1Thrombin binds a receptor on healthy endothelium and stops clotting. Which receptor, and what does it switch on?
Thrombomodulin; it activates protein C, which (with protein S) destroys Va and VIIIa.
A2Which endothelial product is the main clot-breaking signal?
tPA (converts plasminogen to plasmin).

LO 2The cascade, PT and aPTT

Q1. Where are the clotting factors made, and which need vitamin K?
  • All coagulation proteins are made exclusively in hepatocytes, except FVIII
  • Vitamin K–dependent: II, VII, IX, X, protein C, protein S (vitamin K lets them be γ-carboxylated)
FactorNameNote
IFibrinogenCommon pathway
IIProthrombinVit K
IIITissue factorExtrinsic
IVCalciumAll steps
VLabile factorCofactor for Xa; FV Leiden
VIIStable factorVit K; shortest half-life
VIIIAntihemophilic factor ANot from hepatocytes; carried by vWF
IXChristmas factorVit K; hemophilia B
XStuart-ProwerVit K
XI · XII · XIIIAntihemophilic C · Hageman · fibrin-stabilizingXI = hemophilia C

Vitamin K–dependent factors

  • Made in the liver: II, VII, IX, X (+ C, S)
In-house exam

"The only coagulation protein not made in hepatocytes" = Factor VIII.

Step 1

FVIII is made by endothelial cells (liver sinusoids and elsewhere). That is why FVIII stays normal in liver disease but falls in DIC.

Memory tool

Vitamin K factors = "1972": 10, 9, 7, 2 (+ proteins C and S).

Q2. How do the extrinsic, intrinsic and common pathways run?
PathwayHow it startsKey step
Extrinsic"Extrinsic" to plasma: needs tissue damage; key protein = tissue factorTF binds VIIa → TF–VIIa activates X
Intrinsic ("contact")Factors already in blood; XII activated by kallikrein on negatively charged surfaces (platelets)IXa + VIIIa (tenase) activates X
CommonStarts at Xa from either armXa + Va (prothrombinase) → thrombin → fibrin

Cascade with thrombin feedback

  • Green arrows: thrombin activates V, VIII, XI, XIII

Three pathways

  • Intrinsic + extrinsic converge on Xa
Analogy — the spark and the amplifier

The extrinsic pathway is the spark (tissue factor lights the fire). The intrinsic pathway is the amplifier that turns a spark into a blaze of thrombin.

Trap

FXII deficiency → very long aPTT but no bleeding. FXIII deficiency → bleeding (umbilical stump) with normal PT and aPTT.

Q3. What do the PT and aPTT measure, and what prolongs each?

PT → extrinsic

  • Add thromboplastin (tissue factor) + Ca²⁺ to citrated plasma
  • Reported as INR to standardize between labs
  • Prolonged by: liver disease, DIC, vitamin K deficiency, warfarin, FVII deficiency

aPTT → intrinsic

  • Add kaolin + phospholipid + Ca²⁺
  • Prolonged by: heparin, factor deficiency (VIII, IX, XII, XI)
  • Nonspecific inhibitor: lupus anticoagulant
  • Specific inhibitor: acquired FVIII inhibitor

PT

  • Add thromboplastin → VII → X/V → thrombin

aPTT

  • Add kaolin + phospholipid → XII, XI, IX/VIII → X/V
In-house exam

Know the three tests cold: PT → extrinsic, aPTT → intrinsic, thrombin time → common pathway (fibrinogen → fibrin).

Memory tool

"PeT" = PT, extrinsic, tissue factor. "WEPT" = Warfarin, Extrinsic, PT. "HIP" = Heparin, Intrinsic, PTT.

ApplyLO 2 application questions

A1A patient with cirrhosis has a long PT and aPTT. Which factor level would still be normal?
Factor VIII (not made in hepatocytes).
A2A newborn who skipped the vitamin K shot bleeds on day 4. Which test rises first, and why?
PT: FVII has the shortest half-life, so it falls first.

LO 3Plasmin and fibrinolysis

Q1. How does plasmin break down a clot?
  • Normal endothelium sits in an anticoagulant state and makes tPA
  • tPA converts plasminogen → plasmin; plasmin cleaves fibrin and fibrinogen
  • Fibrinolysis keeps the clot sized to the injury: clot formation and clot breakdown stay in balance
Step 1

Alteplase (tPA) dissolves clots. Tranexamic acid / aminocaproic acid block plasminogen activation and protect clots (used in hemophilia and vWD dental bleeding). D-dimer is a sensitive rule-out; ↑ in DVT, PE and DIC.

Analogy — the cleanup crew

Plasmin is the cleanup crew that arrives after the repair. PAI-1 and α2-antiplasmin are the foremen who stop them from tearing the patch out too soon.

ApplyLO 3 application question

A1A hemophilia patient needs a tooth pulled. Which drug class protects the clot in the mouth?
Antifibrinolytics (tranexamic acid or aminocaproic acid), with factor replacement as needed.

LO 4Working up a bleeding patient

Q1. How does the bleeding pattern point to platelets or factors?
Platelet / vWF (primary)Factor (secondary)
WhereSkin + mucosa: petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gums, heavy mensesDeep: joints, muscles, soft tissue, retroperitoneum, brain
WhenImmediately after a cutDelayed, prolonged
PetechiaeYesNo
ExamplesITP, vWD, Bernard-Soulier, GlanzmannHemophilia A/B, vitamin K deficiency, warfarin
High yield

Bleeding into joints → coagulation cascade problem. Bleeding into skin/mucosa → platelet problem.

Q2. Which tests do I order, and how do I read them?
TestChecks
Platelet countNumber
Bleeding time / PFA-100Platelet + vWF function
PT · aPTT · TTExtrinsic · intrinsic · common (fibrinogen → fibrin)
Mixing study (1:1 normal plasma)Corrects → factor deficiency · doesn't → inhibitor (lupus anticoagulant, acquired FVIII inhibitor, heparin)
Factor assaysWhich factor, and how severe
vWF antigen · activity (ristocetin cofactor) · ristocetin aggregationAmount and function of vWF
Fibrinogen · D-dimerConsumption (DIC)
Trap — lupus anticoagulant

It prolongs the aPTT in the tube (binds the phospholipid) and doesn't correct on mixing, but in the body it causes clots and miscarriage (antiphospholipid syndrome).

Memory tool

Mixing study: "add the missing piece." If the patient is just missing a factor, normal plasma fills the gap and the time corrects. If something is attacking the factor, the attacker eats the new plasma too.

vWD type 1N↑NN/↑Corrects↓ vWF Ag + activity

Trap — liver vs DIC

Both prolong PT and aPTT. FVIII normal → liver disease. FVIII low + ↓ fibrinogen + ↑ D-dimer + schistocytes → DIC.

Step 1

DIC causes: SSSTOP making thrombi: heat Stroke, Snake bites, Sepsis, Trauma, Obstetric complications, acute Pancreatitis (+ malignancy, nephrotic syndrome, transfusion).

ApplyLO 4 application questions

A1A 68-year-old woman with no bleeding history has a large thigh hematoma; aPTT 78 that does not correct on mixing; FVIII 2%. Diagnosis?
Acquired hemophilia A (autoantibody against FVIII).
A2A woman has a DVT and a past miscarriage; aPTT 58, not corrected by mixing. Which antibody?
Anticardiolipin / lupus anticoagulant → antiphospholipid syndrome.

LO 5Hemophilia A and B

Q1. What causes hemophilia, and who gets it?
  • "Love of bleeding." Hemophilia A = defective or deficient FVIII; hemophilia B (Christmas disease) = FIX
  • Both X-linked recessive; clinically similar; together ≈ 1 in 5,000 male births
  • Account for >90% of congenital bleeding disorders (lecture); A is about 5× more common than B
  • Mechanism: no tenase (IXa + VIIIa) → weak thrombin burst → unstable clot. Normally vWF carries inactive FVIII; injury releases it to bind FIX
  • ⅓ are new (spontaneous) mutations, as the Haldane hypothesis predicts → a negative family history doesn't exclude it
  • Women are affected rarely: carrier mother + affected father, Turner syndrome (XO), extreme lyonization (chance inactivation of most normal X's)

X-linked recessive

  • Carrier mom → 50% of sons affected, 50% of daughters carriers
In-house exam

Inheritance of hemophilia A and B = X-linked recessive. Hemophilia C (FXI) is autosomal: males and females equal.

Memory tool

"Hemophilia Ate" → A = eight (VIII). B = Christmas (IX: nine days of Christmas left to remember). C = Common to both sexes.

Q2. How does hemophilia present, and how does severity track factor level?
SeverityFactor levelBleeding
Severe<1% of normalSpontaneous bleeding into joints (hemarthroses) and muscles
Moderate1–5%After trauma or surgery; occasionally spontaneous
Mild>5–<40%Only after trauma or surgery
  • Spontaneous joint bleeds, often into one target joint; soft-tissue bleeds after minor trauma
  • Average age of first joint bleed in severe hemophilia ≈ 18 months (when toddlers start walking)
  • Other clues: bleeding after circumcision or from the umbilical stump, hematuria ("pink-tinged urine"), no petechiae
  • Labs: ↑ aPTT, normal PT, platelets and bleeding time; mixing corrects; ↓ factor level

Hemarthrosis

  • Spontaneous bleeding into a target joint

Soft-tissue bleed

  • Large hematoma after minor trauma

Severity by factor level

  • <1% severe · 1–5% moderate · 5–40% mild
High yield

Boy + hemarthroses + isolated ↑ aPTT that corrects on mixing = hemophilia. Untreated, the classic consequence is hemarthroses → joint deformity.

Trap

Hemophilia A and B are clinically identical; only a factor assay separates them. Neither causes petechiae.

Q3. How do hemophilia B and C differ from A?
AB (Christmas)C
FactorVIIIIX (vitamin K–dependent serine protease)XI
InheritanceX-linked recessiveX-linked recessiveAutosomal; M = F
Frequency≈5× B≈1:100,000 malesRare (Ashkenazi Jewish)
BleedingSpontaneous joints/muscles when severeOnly with trauma; no joint/muscle bleeds
NotesMost common hemophiliaMostly point mutations; in 14% FIX is present but non-functionalBleeds at surgery

Hemophilia C

  • Bleeding after trauma; spares joints and muscles
Q4. How is hemophilia treated, and what are the complications?
  • A: FVIII concentrate (prophylaxis), emicizumab, desmopressin if mild (releases stored FVIII + vWF)
  • B: FIX concentrate (desmopressin doesn't help)
  • C: FFP or antifibrinolytics around surgery
  • Adjuncts: tranexamic acid for mucosal/dental bleeding
  • Complications: arthropathy (target joint destroyed), intracranial hemorrhage, inhibitors (alloantibodies against infused factor → bypassing agents)
Step 1

Emicizumab is a bispecific antibody that bridges IXa and X, doing VIII's job, so it works even when the patient has FVIII inhibitors.

ApplyLO 5 application questions

A1A 2-month-old boy bruises when his mother touches him, has pink urine, and his umbilical stump bled for days. aPTT 100 s, PT 10 s. Mom is adopted. Diagnosis and next test?
Hemophilia A most likely (more common than B). Next: mixing study (corrects) → FVIII and FIX assays. Unknown family history fits the ⅓ new-mutation rate, too.
A2A woman's father has hemophilia A. What is the chance her son is affected?
50%. She is an obligate carrier; each son has a 50% chance, each daughter a 50% chance of being a carrier.
A3Why is acquired hemophilia unlikely in that 2-month-old?
It is rare at that age, and the bleeding has been present since birth (umbilical stump), pointing to an inherited defect.

LO 6von Willebrand disease vs hemophilia A

Q1. What does vWF do, and what goes wrong in vWD?
  • vWF has two jobs: (1) glue: bridges platelet GPIb to subendothelial collagen (adhesion) and helps platelet–platelet binding; (2) bodyguard: carries and protects FVIII
  • vWD = ↓ amount or ↓ function of vWF → poor adhesion (mucosal bleeding) ± low FVIII (mild ↑ aPTT)
  • Most common inherited bleeding disorder (≈1%); mostly autosomal dominant → males and females

Normal vs vWD

  • Without vWF, platelets don't stick at the tear

Autosomal dominant

  • Types 1 and 2: sons and daughters equally
Analogy — the glue and the bodyguard

vWF is glue for platelets and a bodyguard for FVIII. Lose the glue → skin and mucosal bleeding. Lose the bodyguard → FVIII is cleared faster and the aPTT creeps up.

Q2. What are the vWD types?
TypeDefectKey point
1Partial quantitative deficiencyMost common; mild; DDAVP works
2AQualitative: loss of high-molecular-weight multimers↓ platelet-dependent function
2BQualitative: ↑ affinity for GPIbClumps platelets → thrombocytopenia; ↑ aggregation to low-dose ristocetin; DDAVP worsens it → give donor vWF
2MQualitative: ↓ platelet-dependent function, normal multimers—
2NQualitative: can't bind FVIIILow FVIII; mimics hemophilia A
3Complete deficiencySevere; very low FVIII; joint bleeds like hemophilia

Classification

  • 1 = less · 2 = broken · 3 = none
Memory tool

"1 = less, 2 = broken, 3 = none." 2B = Binds platelets too well (and Bad with DDAVP). 2N = No FVIII binding.

Step 1

Type 3 is usually autosomal recessive. Acquired vWD shows up with aortic stenosis (shear destroys large multimers; Heyde syndrome with GI angiodysplasia bleeding).

Q3. How is vWD diagnosed?
  • PT normal, platelet count normal (mildly low in 2B), aPTT normal or ↑ (if FVIII low), bleeding time ↑
  • vWF antigen assay → amount of vWF protein
  • vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor assay) → function
  • Platelet aggregation testing → no aggregation to ristocetin (corrected by adding normal plasma, unlike Bernard-Soulier)

Aggregometry

  • vWD: flat line with ristocetin

vWD summary

  • Easy bruising, mucosal bleeding; treat with DDAVP
Trap

Normal PT, aPTT and platelets do not rule out vWD. A normal "baseline panel" in a patient with mucosal bleeding means order vWF studies.

Q4. How do I tell vWD from hemophilia A?
vWDHemophilia A
Defect↓ or abnormal vWF (→ secondary ↓ FVIII)↓ or abnormal FVIII
InheritanceAutosomal dominant (mostly)X-linked recessive
WhoMales and femalesAlmost always males
BleedingMucocutaneous: bruising, epistaxis, heavy menses, dentalDeep: joints, muscles; delayed
Bleeding time↑Normal
PT / aPTTN / N or ↑N / ↑
vWF · ristocetin↓ · ↓N · N
TreatmentDesmopressin, vWF concentrate, TXA, hormonal therapy for mensesFVIII; DDAVP if mild

vWD bleeding

  • Epistaxis and easy bruising
High yield

Normal platelet count + ↑ bleeding time + mildly ↑ aPTT + ↓ ristocetin cofactor = vWD. Classic consequence: excessive bleeding after oral surgery or tooth extraction.

Step 1

Desmopressin (DDAVP) releases vWF and FVIII stored in endothelial Weibel-Palade bodies.

ApplyLO 6 application questions

A1A 12-year-old girl's periods last 8–10 days (12+ pads/day); she had childhood nosebleeds and bruises easily; dad bled for days after wisdom teeth. PT, aPTT and platelets normal. Diagnosis and tests?
von Willebrand disease (autosomal dominant: dad affected). Order vWF antigen, vWF activity (ristocetin cofactor) and ristocetin aggregation.
A2A patient with vWD is given desmopressin and their platelet count drops sharply. Which type?
Type 2B: the abnormal vWF binds GPIb too well and clears platelets. Give donor vWF instead.

LO 7Factor V Leiden

Q1. What does normal Factor V do?

Procoagulant

  • Va binds Xa (prothrombinase) → speeds thrombin generation

Anticoagulant control

  • Activated protein C cleaves Va at specific sites → inactivates it → slows thrombin and limits clot size

FV deficiency → bleeding. Some FV mutations (FV Leiden) instead → thrombosis.

Q2. How does the Leiden mutation cause clots?

Normal vs APC resistance

  • Leiden Va is not cut → clot keeps growing
In-house exam

"G to A at 1691," "R506Q," "APC resistance" all = Factor V Leiden.

Memory tool

"Leiden = Lasting": Va lasts because APC can't cut it. R → Q: the APC scissors need the R.

Analogy — the stuck accelerator

Va is the gas pedal; APC lifts your foot off. In FV Leiden the pedal is jammed: the brake pulls, but the pedal won't come up.

Q3. Who has it, and what does it cause?
GroupHeterozygous frequency
General US / European3–8% (low thrombosis risk)
Caucasian Americans5.2%
Hispanic Americans2.2%
Native Americans1.25%
African Americans1.2%
Asian Americans0.45%
Homozygous1:5,000 (much higher risk)
  • Extremely rare in Asian, African and Indigenous Australian populations
  • Clinical: spontaneous venous thrombosis, usually at a young age: any extremity (DVT), pulmonary vasculature, portal and mesenteric veins
  • Triggers stack on top: estrogen (OCPs), pregnancy, surgery
  • PT and aPTT are normal; diagnose with APC resistance assay → PCR

DVT

  • Thrombus in deep leg veins (popliteal, femoral)

DVT clinically

  • Swollen, red, tender calf
Step 1 — other inherited thrombophilias
  • FV Leiden: most common inherited thrombophilia; DVT, cerebral vein thrombosis, recurrent pregnancy loss
  • Prothrombin G20210A: 3′ UTR mutation → ↑ prothrombin; 2nd most common
  • Protein C/S deficiency: can't inactivate Va/VIIIa; warfarin skin necrosis
  • Antithrombin deficiency: heparin fails to raise aPTT; can be acquired in nephrotic syndrome
High yield

Think thrombophilia: young patient with DVT/PE, unusual sites (portal, mesenteric, cerebral), recurrent clots, strong family history.

ApplyLO 7 application questions

A1A 26-year-old on OCPs has a left-leg DVT; her mother had a PE at 40. Her plasma shows APC resistance. Diagnosis and mutation?
Factor V Leiden: G→A at 1691, R506Q in factor V.
A2Warfarin is started without heparin; on day 3 painful dark skin patches appear. Underlying deficiency?
Protein C deficiency (protein C falls fast on warfarin → transient hypercoagulable state → skin necrosis).

MCQExam-style questions

Score: 0 / 0

1A 2-month-old boy bruises whenever his mother picks him up and has pink-tinged urine. His umbilical stump took several days to stop bleeding. aPTT 100 s (21–30), PT 10 s (7–12). Most likely diagnosis?

Isolated ↑ aPTT + deep/GU bleeding in a male infant → hemophilia, most likely A (FVIII). Thrombocytopenia wouldn't prolong the aPTT; vitamin K deficiency raises the PT first.

2A 12-year-old girl has periods lasting 8–10 days, past nosebleeds and easy bruising. Her father bled repeatedly after wisdom-tooth extraction. PT, aPTT and platelets are normal. Most likely diagnosis?

Mucocutaneous bleeding in a girl, affected father (AD) and normal baseline labs → vWD. Hemophilia A is X-linked and causes deep bleeds.

3A 23-year-old woman bruises easily. Platelets 229,000; PT 12 s; PTT 38 s, corrected by a 1:1 mix. Ristocetin-induced aggregation is markedly reduced. Which is most likely in her future?

vWD → mucosal bleeding, classically after dental work. Hemarthroses fit hemophilia.

4An 11-year-old boy has easy bruising and a pharyngeal hemorrhage after a tonsil injury; several male relatives bleed. PT 13 s; PTT 52 s, corrected by mixing. Without treatment, which complication is most likely?

X-linked bleeding + ↑ PTT that corrects → hemophilia A → joint bleeds and arthropathy. Factor disorders don't cause petechiae.

5A 33-year-old woman has her second DVT in 2 years and a past first-trimester miscarriage. Platelets 180,000; PT normal; aPTT 58 s; a mixing study does not correct. Which antibody is most likely?

Antiphospholipid syndrome: long aPTT that doesn't correct, yet the patient clots and miscarries. Anti-FVIII causes bleeding, not clots.

6A 26-year-old woman on oral contraceptives develops a left-leg DVT; her mother had a PE at 40. PT and aPTT are normal. Her plasma shows resistance to activated protein C. The underlying mutation is best described as:

Factor V Leiden: G→A at 1691 → R506Q at an APC cleavage site → Va resists inactivation.

7Which coagulation protein is not synthesized in hepatocytes?

FVIII comes from endothelial cells, so it stays normal in liver disease.

8Which test measures the final common step, fibrinogen → fibrin?

PT → extrinsic, aPTT → intrinsic, thrombin time → common pathway.

9On intact endothelium, thrombin binds thrombomodulin. What is the main result?

Thrombin–thrombomodulin loses its clotting function and becomes an anticoagulant by activating protein C.

10A woman's father has hemophilia A; her husband is unaffected. What is the chance that their son will have hemophilia A?

She is an obligate carrier (got her father's X). Each son has a 50% chance.

11Warfarin is started for a DVT without heparin bridging. On day 3 painful, dark, necrotic skin patches appear on the thighs. Which deficiency is most likely?

Protein C has a short half-life; warfarin drops it first → transient hypercoagulability → warfarin skin necrosis.

12A 68-year-old woman with no bleeding history has a large thigh hematoma. PT normal; aPTT 78 s, not corrected by mixing; FVIII 2%. Most likely diagnosis?

New bleeding in an older adult + long aPTT that doesn't correct + low FVIII → acquired hemophilia A. Lupus anticoagulant causes clots, not hematomas.

13A patient with von Willebrand disease receives desmopressin before surgery, and her platelet count falls sharply. Which vWD type does she have?

Type 2B: vWF with ↑ affinity for GPIb; releasing more of it clumps and clears platelets. Treat with donor vWF.
